questions.question: Define development aid and development co-operation, and describe the three types of aid named in the syllabus with an example and a weakness of each.
questions.expected_answer: Development aid is the transfer of resources — money, goods, technology or expertise — from richer countries and institutions to poorer ones on terms softer than the market's, as grants or concessional loans; it flows bilaterally between governments, multilaterally through institutions like the World Bank and UN agencies, and through NGOs such as Gift of the Givers. Development co-operation reframes the relationship as a partnership with obligations on both sides: recipients set priorities and account for results, and donors align with the recipient's own plans rather than scattering their own projects. The three types: technical aid transfers knowledge and skills — engineers designing water schemes, doctors training rural nurses — with the strength that a skill keeps working after money is spent once, and the weakness that experts can fly in and out leaving no local capacity. Conditional or tied aid attaches strings: procurement tying forces the recipient to buy the donor's goods, recycling money back to the donor and inflating costs, while policy conditionality — the structural adjustment programmes of the 1980s and 1990s — required spending cuts and privatisation that gutted many African health and education budgets. Humanitarian aid is emergency relief — food, water, shelter and medicine after disasters like cyclone Idai or the KwaZulu-Natal floods; it saves lives fast but treats symptoms by design, and prolonged food aid can undercut local farmers.

questions.question: Present the positive case for development aid using specific case studies, including South Africa's experience, and state the conditions under which aid succeeds.
questions.expected_answer: Aid's strongest evidence is in health: the aid-funded global vaccination campaign eradicated smallpox entirely, polio has been pushed to the edge of extinction, and malaria deaths fell steeply where insecticide-treated nets and treatment were rolled out. In South Africa, PEPFAR and Global Fund financing helped carry the world's largest antiretroviral programme, and life expectancy, which had collapsed into the low fifties at the epidemic's peak, climbed back above sixty — millions of measurable lives. Humanitarian relief works when speed and logistics are right, as Gift of the Givers showed reaching flood-hit KwaZulu-Natal within days, and as the 2014 Ebola response showed in West Africa. Technical and infrastructure aid built roads, water schemes and power lines that private capital would not risk, trained nurses, teachers and engineers, and the aid-funded Green Revolution research helped Asia escape recurring famine; grants can also catalyse private investment many times their size by de-risking major projects. The pattern across the successes: aid works best when targeted at specific, measurable problems — a disease, a road, a skill — aligned with the recipient's own priorities, and sustained long enough to finish the job.

questions.question: Present the negative case against development aid — dependency, distortion, debt and conditionality — with mechanisms and examples, and conclude with a balanced verdict.
questions.expected_answer: Dependency: when aid finances a large share of a government's budget year after year, accountability tilts toward donors rather than citizens and the urgency of building a domestic tax base fades — the bridge becomes a crutch. Distortion: free or subsidised food aid delivered outside genuine emergencies undercuts local farmers until they stop planting, manufacturing the shortages it was meant to relieve; donor projects also hire away the best local staff at salaries ministries cannot match, and cheap imports such as second-hand clothing have been blamed for smothering African textile industries. Debt: loans called aid must be repaid, and in the 1980s and 1990s many African countries paid more in debt service than they spent on health and education combined, until international campaigns forced relief for heavily indebted poor countries — proof that the grant-loan distinction decides whether aid lifts or sinks. Conditionality added its own costs: structural adjustment gutted clinics and classrooms, and tied procurement inflated invoices while recycling money to donor firms; corruption and fragmentation — hundreds of small projects exhausting small ministries — complete the charge sheet. The balanced verdict: aid is a tool, not a verdict — powerful against specific solvable problems, dangerous as a permanent economic strategy. It should work like scaffolding: essential during construction, designed from day one to come down as the building stands.
